newsitem.title: GUATEMALA: Guatemalan rebels cheered on return from exile.
newsitem.headline: Guatemalan rebels cheered on return from exile.

text.p: Left-wing rebel commanders returned to Guatemala after years in exile on Saturday and were greeted by hundreds of ecstatic supporters hailing the end of a brutal 36-year civil war.

On the eve of a landmark peace treaty with the government, leaders of four factions of the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) flew into Guatemala City from Mexico, saying it was years since they had set eyes on the capital.
"I am profoundly moved to the depths of my soul by such a warm reception," Carlos Gonzalez, one of the URNG leaders, told an airport news conference.

The veteran rebels, who became emotional as cheers filled the airport's arrivals hall, were optimistic about the peace treaty, and said their aim was to form a political party with support from unions and other friends who greeted them. They said they had no fears for their safety.
Almost as remarkable as the appearance of the rebel commanders, some who have lived in exile in Mexico since the 1960s, was the unbridled support of civilians.
"These men are visionaries. They had the courage to change the destiny of us Guatemalans," said a cheering woman, Alma Cruz, flanked by other supporters of the rebels waving URNG banners and flags.

In a war in which 140,000 people were killed, many of them leftists brutally massacred by the army or dragged from their homes and "disappeared", professing open support for the rebels was once considered a virtual death sentence.

Though the repression has ebbed in the 1990s, Saturday's show of support was unprecedented. Radio stations reporting from the airport urged listeners to forget who started the war and think only of the future.
Indians wearing colourful traditional dresses burned candles on an altar for peace, as airport taxi drivers struggled to make sense of the bizarre scene.

Nobel Peace Prize winner Rigoberta Menchu, herself a Mayan in a country where 60 percent of the population are Indian, shed tears as she embraced the guerrillas, Pablo Monsanto, Rolando Moran, Gonzalez and Jorge Rosal.
Rosal was taking the place of his commander, Gaspar Ilom, who was banned from the peace ceremony after his forces kidnapped a Guatemalan woman in violation of the peace accords.
The rebels were welcomed in Guatemala by the government peace commission, including an army general, and mediators from the United Nations who have brokered talks since 1994.

President Alvaro Arzu, who has won national and international acclaim for ending the war less than a year after taking office, met his Spanish counterpart Jose Maria Aznar in a nearby air force base but skipped greeting the rebels.

Outgoing U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali was due to arrive later, and on Sunday Latin American heads of state were scheduled to fly in for the gala peace ceremony scheduled for 5 p.m. (6 p.m. EST/2300 GMT) at the National Palace.
Rebel troops, however, who number 1,700 and are still hidden in camps in the mountains, were not expected to march into Guatemala City for the peace treaty.
They say they will watch it on television, and start demobilizing in 1997.
